children: founder and Chief Executive Patrick Dovigi said he intends to continue leading the waste-management company and retain his entire ownership stake regardless of the outcome of its strategic review.

Dovigi’s comments shift attention toward management continuity and the company’s long-term prospects after months of speculation about GFL’s ownership. He described the business as being only in the “third inning” of its development and said he remains confident in its outlook.

“I just feel really good about where the company is,” Dovigi said during an appearance Wednesday on Bloomberg Deals TV. He added that he has no intention of stepping away from a company he has led for nearly two decades.

For investors, Dovigi’s willingness to reinvest all his equity in any potential transaction signals that he believes GFL’s future value could exceed its current public-market valuation. The company’s shares have declined 3.7% this year, leaving it with a market capitalization of about $18 billion.

Dovigi founded GFL in 2007 with backing from private equity investors. The company has since expanded across all 10 Canadian provinces and 26 U.S. states, becoming North America’s fourth-largest diversified environmental-services provider.

GFL also simplified its portfolio last year when Apollo Global Management and BC Partners acquired a controlling interest in its environmental-services division. That transaction gave the company additional capital and sharpened its focus on its core solid-waste operations.

The board formed a special committee in July to evaluate preliminary expressions of interest and oversee related discussions. Dovigi said no decision has been reached and emphasized that the company would weigh any opportunity based on its potential benefit to shareholders.
“We’re shareholders first and we like to explore all opportunities for all of our shareholders,” he said.

title: GFL CEO signals long-term commitment as investors reassess waste hauler
